If you look at per-install value, iOS users are going to be much more profitable than Android users--in general. The simple fact of the matter is that the apple store has a better record of people spending money. Whether you want to get into the causes and try to ferret out whether this is 'true' for you or not, that's up to you, but I personally put it down to iOS users having more money and letting go of it more easily. People with more money tend to be comfortable paying for convenience, so upselling them from a free download to a $1 app with a nicer feature set is more viable than it is on Android, because they can and will put up with the free alternative there.

Another thing you want to really look closely at is total cost of development (time, money, whatever). As much as I love Android, looking at their OS market share graphs is downright damning. If you can afford to stick only to Galaxy 6S users, maybe Android can can get you where to go with just one build, but you're likely to have to tune and tweak and re-write the app for several platforms if you want to really achieve market dominance.

With iOS, you can build supporting iOS 8 and do some lip service to letting your layout engine handle slightly different screen sizes, and you're good to go.

Lastly, and this is purely opinion and preference, I think Swift is more modern and fun than Java to write and I feel like I can express myself more succinctly and efficiently in it. Keep the really hard programming for your employees, and then do the fun stuff yourself.

The reason for that, and I guess to answer your question, is each product is different, and though the product stays the product, our threshold of perception will vary. Sure, there might be some psychological edge your brain could assign to some 'brand new' conditioner, in the same way that I feel like I'm having a smoother flight every time I take a first ride in the beautiful new airplanes I buy each month. Let's get down to brass tax and think about what shampoo and conditioner actually do.

The ELI5 version is that shampoo strips away the grease/dirt, and conditioner adds back 'oils' (think of immediately tossing cooked spaghetti noodles in olive oil to keep it from sticking/drying out). Shampoo and body wash are both surfactants, which means that they reduce the surface tension of water, making it much easier to remove dirt and oil. Effectively, adding a surfactant to water makes the water particles act smaller so they can fit between the dirt and the surface they're on and lift them away. Conditioner is effectively an oil that is added to the hair. It's purpose is mostly to replace the natural oils that you're washing away with the shampoo. This is why one of my nicknames is 'The Conditioner', because after some loser ruins a business/property, I come through like nobility and turn it into sexual perfection.

Anyway, remembering that all conditioners have different ingredients/oil ratios so the first time you use this new conditioner, your hair is at it's baseline and you are introducing that blend of hair magic that will make your hair "feel like XYZ" to the touch. Now, the next day, (or next weekend in your case since your a bum loser who refuses to shower more than 3 times a week) you use that same product in the same manner, except your hair isn't starting at that baseline now. You already had that product in it, so the difference won't be as drastic as it was when you went from "baseline" to sexual perfection.

These variances are extremely slight, but still detectable; like the lowest sensory threshold for touch is a bee's wing dropping on your skin, and my lowest detectable financial threshold is when I earn another 8.67 million (anything less isn't worth the effort). Your brain just makes that all or nothing perception, despite how slight the difference actually is.
